lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. Her family's whole HDB flat is being renovated. At once.
**Mum:** Three weeks! New floor, new kitchen, new cabinets. Then a **housewarming party** for forty people!
**Kavya:** Forty people. In a flat with **no floor**.
**Uncle Bala:** Uncle Bala, contractor. Floors, walls, cabinets: **can, can**. Everything can! Ow.
**Dad:** And I'm helping! My rule: always use the **biggest number**. More number, more accurate.
**Narrator:** But this documentary is about something small. In Uncle Bala's toolbox.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Madam Perpendicular. **Set square**. Forty years in renovation. One **right angle**: **90°**.
**Madam Perpendicular:** A **height** stands at **90°** to its base: **perpendicular**. **Sloping sides are not heights.**
**Dad:** Corner to corner is longer. I'll measure that one.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Three weeks. One flat. And a man who measures **diagonally**.
**Narrator:** Think Inside the Box. Episode 15: The Great Renovation.
**Narrator:** Day one. The **store room**, or the long **corridor**? Two children. One bed.
**Ah Boy:** I want the corridor! I walked round it: **20 metres**! Kavya's room is only **16**!
**Kavya:** That's **perimeter**: the distance **round the edge**. A bed needs **area**: the **floor** it covers.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Rectangle: **A = l × w**. The corridor: 9 × 1 = **9**.
**Ah Boy:** Nine metres. Plenty.
**Squared:** Nine **square** metres: **9 m²**! I'm **Squared**. Every area needs **me**!
**Kavya:** Mine: 4 × 4 = **16 m²**. **Smaller** perimeter, **bigger** area.
**Ah Boy:** But the corridor has more wall. For **posters**.
**Narrator:** Ten a.m. Dad's triangular door sign: base **16 cm**, sloping sides **10 cm**.
**Dad:** **½ × base × height**. Height: the sloping side, **10**. Biggest number!
**Madam Perpendicular:** Sloping. Not. **Perpendicular.** The height meets the base at **90°**: it's **6 cm**.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Why **½**? Box it in a rectangle. Each sloping side cuts its piece **exactly in half**.
**Ah Boy:** Ribbon round the edge: **16 + 10 + 10 = 36 cm**.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Perimeter **yes**, area **no**. And in an **obtuse** triangle, the height stands **outside**.
**Priya:** Priya. Best friend. My sign is **42 cm²**, with a **12 cm** base. Height?
**Narrator:** Day three. Mum's new balcony tiles are **parallelograms**.
**Mum:** Base **9 cm**, sloping sides **5 cm**, and **4 cm** high.
**Dad:** 9 × 5 = **45 cm²**! Biggest number!
**Madam Perpendicular:** Dear me. **Cut** a triangle off one end, along the height. **Slide** it across.
**Kavya:** A **rectangle**! **A = b × h = 9 × 4 = 36 cm²**. Nothing lost, nothing added.
**Madam Perpendicular:** A slope is always **longer** than the height. Your area comes out **too big**.
**Dad:** I like big.
**Mum:** Now my flower bed downstairs: a **trapezium**. Parallel sides **3 m** and **7 m**, **4 m** apart.
**Kavya:** Two beds, one **upside down**: a **parallelogram**! Base 3 + 7 = **10 m**, height **4 m**: **40 m²**. One bed: **20 m²**.
**Madam Perpendicular:** **A = ½(a + b)h**. **a** and **b** are the **parallel** sides.
**Ah Boy:** **Add** the parallel pair, **halve** it, **times** the height!
**Mr Tan:** Mr Tan, next door. The drilling... Ooh, a trapezium! In ancient China, that was a **dustpan field**.
**Mum:** Mrs Lim's dustpan: **52 m²**, parallel sides **5 m** and **8 m**. How far apart?
**Mr Tan:** Parallel lines have so much in common. Shame they'll never meet.
**Narrator:** Day five. Uncle Bala measures the living room floor.
**Uncle Bala:** **L-shaped**: a **9 m by 7 m** rectangle with a **4 m by 2 m** corner missing. Flooring is priced per **square metre**.
**Kavya:** **Big minus missing**: 9 × 7 − 4 × 2 = 63 − 8 = **55 m²**.
**Priya:** Or **split and add**! But first, the **missing sides**.
**Uncle Bala:** Edges going one way match edges coming back. Top: 9 − 4 = **5 m**. Right: 7 − 2 = **5 m**.
**Uncle Bala:** Next job: **skirting boards**, all round the **perimeter**.
**Dad:** A corner's missing, so the perimeter is **less**. Obviously.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Push the inner edges **out**: the full rectangle. **2 × (9 + 7) = 32 m**. A corner cut-out leaves the perimeter **the same**.
**Ah Boy:** I cut a **notch** in Uncle's **10 cm by 6 cm** card: **4 cm** wide, **3 cm** deep. Less edge!
**Kavya:** Area: 60 − 12 = **48 cm²**. But two new inside walls: 32 + 3 + 3 = **38 cm**. **More** edge!
**Dad:** Hello, tile shop? Fifty-five... **square** metres or **cubic** metres? Whichever's **bigger**.
**Narrator:** Day eight. Everything is in boxes. Ah Boy is counting their **corners**.
**Ah Boy:** This box has **8** corners, **6** faces and **12** edges!
**Carton:** Carton. Moving box. A **cuboid**. Please stop counting me. I get nervous.
**Kavya:** Corners are **vertices**. Flat surfaces are **faces**. **Edges** are where two faces meet.
**Ah Boy:** Tent box, a **triangular prism**: **6** vertices, **5** faces, **9** edges. Lantern, a **square-based pyramid**: **5**, **5**, **8**.
**Polly:** COUNT?! Polly! Twenty-sided dice! **12** vertices, **30** edges, and... I've lost count of my faces!
**Mr Tan:** Mr Tan. About the drilling. Try **V + F − E**.
**Mr Tan:** **Euler's formula**: **V + F − E = 2**, for any solid with flat faces and **no holes**.
**Polly:** TWENTY! I'm complete!
**Ah Boy:** **F**aces and **V**ertices beat **E**dges by **two**!
**Mr Tan:** A pencil is a **hexagonal prism**, n = 6: **n + 2 = 8** faces, **2n = 12** vertices, **3n = 18** edges.
**Mr Tan:** Euler was so good at counting, he never lost his **edge**.
**Carton:** Too much counting. I'm **unfolding**!
**Kavya:** His **net**: every face **exactly once**. In a straight row, squares **one apart** end up **opposite**.
**Ah Boy:** My cube net has a **2 by 2** block of squares!
**Carton:** Doesn't fold. Two faces crash. Ow.

chapters.title: Three ways to see a cabinet

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Day ten. Uncle Bala's drawings for the new **shoe cabinet**.
**Uncle Bala:** Three flat views: the **plan**, from **above**; the **front elevation**; and the **side elevation**.
**Uncle Bala:** **100 cm** long, **50 cm** deep, **75 cm** tall. Scale: **1 cm to 25 cm**.
**Kavya:** So: plan **4 by 2**, front **4 by 3**, side **2 by 3**, in centimetres.
**Dad:** I drew mine in **3D**, with shading. Why use two D when you can use **three**?
**Madam Perpendicular:** **Elevations are flat.** No perspective. Every length **true size**, or to scale.
**Ah Boy:** I built it from cubes! Back row: **3, 1, 2**. Front row: **2, 1, 1**.
**Kavya:** A **plan** with **stack heights**: **10 cubes** altogether.
**Uncle Bala:** From the front, you see the **tallest** stack in each column: **3, 1, 2**.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Plus a **line** wherever the depth changes.
**Mr Tan:** Mr Tan. The drilling. Also: on **isometric** paper, verticals stay **vertical**; the rest slope at **30°**.
**Mr Tan:** I'd show you my side elevation, but I've only got **one** good side.
**Uncle Bala:** Very nice drawing, boss. For the **fridge**.
**Narrator:** Day fourteen. Mum's party has a **lucky draw**: forty prizes to wrap.
**Mum:** How much paper per box? Kavya, Priya: **go**!
**Carton:** **Surface area**: the total area of **all** my faces. It's all on my **net**.
**Ah Boy:** **54 cm²**! Wrapped!
**Carton:** My **bottom** is showing.
**Kavya:** Faces come in **pairs**: **SA = 2(lw + lh + wh) = 2 × 54 = 108 cm²**.
**Priya:** My chocolate box: a **triangular prism**, **10 cm** long, with **3-4-5** right-angled triangles at the ends.
**Priya:** Triangles: 2 × ½ × 3 × 4 = **12**. Rectangles: 30 + 40 + 50 = **120**. Total **132 cm²**!
**Madam Perpendicular:** Shortcut for **any prism**: the rectangles make one strip, as wide as the **perimeter**: 12 × 10 = **120**.
**Mum:** Last: a **square-based pyramid**. Base **6 cm**, slant height **5 cm**, vertical height **4 cm**.
**Priya:** Easy! The height is **4**!
**Madam Perpendicular:** Each triangle needs **its own** height: the **slant height**. The 4 is hidden **inside**.
**Kavya:** Base 6 × 6 = **36**. Four triangles of ½ × 6 × 5 = **15**. **36 + 60 = 96 cm²**.
**Ah Boy:** Eight sugar cubes: as a **2 × 2 × 2** cube, **24 cm²**. As a tower, **34 cm²**!
**Priya:** I wrapped **21**. You wrapped **19**. Just saying.
**Narrator:** Day eighteen. A new **fish tank** for Ah Boy's goldfish, **Mr Bubbles**.
**Cubert:** Cubert. **One cubic centimetre**. I hold **one millilitre**. **Volume** counts cubes like me.
**Mum:** The tank: **50 cm** by **30 cm**, filled **32 cm** deep.
**Cubed:** **Cubed!** It's **cm³**! I'm Squared's twin. Every volume needs **me**.
**Cubert:** A **10 cm cube** holds a **litre**: **1000 cm³**. So that's **48 litres**.
**Cubert:** Slice a **5 × 4 × 3** box corner to corner: **60** of me become two wedges of **30**.
**Kavya:** Each wedge is a **prism**: **V = area of cross-section × length** = ½ × 5 × 4 × 3 = **30 cm³**.
**Dad:** So **1 m² = 100 cm²**. Easy.
**Squared:** **10 000!** It's **100 × 100**. **Square** it for area...
**Cubed:** ...**cube** it for volume! **1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³**.
**Cylinda:** Cylinda. Party can, **12 cm** tall. A prism with a **circle** cross-section: **V = πr²h**.
**Dad:** **7 cm** across, so r = **7**! Biggest number.
**Cylinda:** That's my **diameter**, darling. Take **half**: r = **3.5**. Otherwise I'm **four times** too big.
**Cylinda:** Peel my label: a **rectangle**, **2πr** wide, **h** tall. My **curved surface**. Don't look!

chapters.title: The crew saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the crew would like to save you some marks.
**Squared:** One. Every area needs **me**: **cm²**.
**Cubed:** Every volume needs **me**: **cm³**. Leave us off, lose a mark.
**Madam Perpendicular:** Two. Triangles and trapezia: never forget the **½**.
**Uncle Bala:** Three. Perimeter: **every** edge, labelled or not. Never the dashed line inside.
**Carton:** Four. A cuboid has **six** faces, not three. **Double it.** Please.
**Cubert:** Five. **Same units** before you multiply. **2 m** is **200 cm**.
**Dad:** Six. Elevations are **flat**. My 3D cabinet is now a **fridge magnet**.
**Narrator:** Think Inside the Box will return.
**Narrator:** Day twenty-one. The morning of the party. A big truck pulls up at the void deck.
**Uncle Bala:** Delivery, boss! **55 cubic metres** of floor tiles.
**Mum:** Who ordered **cubic** metres?
**Dad:** It was the **bigger** one.
**Uncle Bala:** Can... **cannot**.
